newsitem.title: UK: Fears grow over Russia's nuclear arsenal.
newsitem.headline: Fears grow over Russia's nuclear arsenal.

text.p: By Nicholas Doughty, Diplomatic Correspondent
Dire warnings from Moscow about the safety and control of Russia's nuclear arsenal are increasingly justified given the chaos in the military, Western experts say.
Russian Defence Minister Igor Rodionov said on Thursday the cash-starved armed forces were in such a parlous state that it was possible nuclear missiles and systems could not be controlled in future.
Analysts and diplomats say his comments were an attempt to win more money for the military machine which once struck fear into the heart of NATO but proved unable even to win the war in Chechnya.
Rodionov's remarks also underline Moscow's chief argument against NATO plans to take in new members from Eastern Europe -- that such expansion would further upset a fragile situation in Russia.
But, even allowing for politics, experts say there are serious concerns about the Russian nuclear arsenal, the world's largest.
Those concerns range from how the weapons are controlled and guarded to maintenance and launch procedures, all of which are shrouded in secrecy by a sensitive Russian military establishment.

"The Russians have tried to play this down and reassure the Americans, but it's clear there is a very serious problem," said Professor Christoph Bluth, an expert on the issue at Britain's Reading University.
"We are seeing a major deterioration in Russian nuclear security," said Dan Plesch of the private British American Security Information Council (BASIC).
Following huge cuts in the superpowers' nuclear arsenals at the end of the Cold War, one of the biggest problems seems to be that no one -- including the Russians -- has an accurate weapons count.
Western estimates say the Russians now have anywhere between 9,000 and 21,000 operational nuclear warheads, of which about 6,000 are long-range.

Thousands are being dismantled under arms control agreements, most of them short-range tactical nuclear weapons which were withdrawn from deployment in 1992 and are held in storage sites all over Russia.
"The biggest problem, also for the Russians, is actually knowing what is in the inventory," said Eric Arnett of the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI).
"Disarmament put a huge strain on the system and the fear is that some small nuclear weapon might just disappear from the inventory."
Experts say the strategic rocket forces which handle the long-range missiles are reasonably secure, although there have been reports of increasing discontent among staff at missile bases.

Low morale and poor living conditions have bred much wider discontent among naval personnel at the key bases around Murmansk and Vladivostok, where most of the nuclear-armed submarines now languish in port.
Long-range nuclear missiles require complex codes and authorisation to fire but Western experts say there are concerns and incomplete information about how the chain of command works.

"To keep the arsenal credible they have to be ready for a strike in a very short time," said one Western official. "That means, given current circumstances, that they might think of removing some of the safeguards in the system to keep it credible."
The older tactical weapons designed for use on the battlefield pose a much bigger problem, since they do not have such elaborate, built-in safety mechanisms.
They are also small and easily hidden. A nuclear artillery shell fits easily in the boot of a car.
"The Russians have dumped these in storage sites and we don't really know how many have been dismantled and how well they are guarded," said Bluth.
Western countries fear that, as a result, nuclear weapons or components could be sold or smuggled out to countries with nuclear ambitions, or that there might even be an accidental missile launch.
The United States has led international efforts to improve nuclear security in Russia but officials say it has been hampered by Moscow's reluctance to expose the secrets of its nuclear arsenal.
